main.title: F-Zero: GP Legend
main.subtitle: The animated series reaches the starting grid
main.summary: F-Zero: GP Legend is Suzak's Game Boy Advance racing game connected with the animated series of the same name. Familiar pilots and newcomers compete in high-speed machines on courses seen from a rotating overhead perspective. Story events give selected racers individual situations, while the Grand Prix provides the broader championship structure. The television connection gives the drivers more narrative context without changing the central challenge of learning a dangerous track. A good race still depends on preserving control through narrow turns and choosing when an opportunity for more speed is actually safe.

cards.heading: Read the surface before taking the jump
cards.text: Tracks combine useful features and hazards, including dash plates, jump plates, rumble strips and minefields. A jump can extend a route but also damage the machine if the landing is mishandled. Adjusting the nose during descent helps control that return to the surface. These details make a racing line more than the shortest distance between corners. A player must recognise what the next section of track will do to the vehicle, then prepare the movement that allows its speed to remain useful after the immediate obstacle has been crossed.

cards.heading: A character has a race to explain
cards.text: Story mode connects individual drivers with a succession of racing situations, giving the cast associated with the anime another way to appear in play. Other modes allow attention to move back toward championship progress or a particular course. The Japanese release also supported e-Reader cards that supplied additional machines, courses and challenges. These different arrangements expand the same racing foundation rather than replacing it, allowing the handheld game to serve both as another visit to the animated setting and as a collection of high-speed courses to understand through repeated attempts.

main.title: Golden Joystick Awards 2003
main.summary: The Golden Joystick Awards, with every category winner of the 2003 edition.

cards.heading: The players' awards
cards.text: The Golden Joystick Awards celebrate games through a public vote, bringing players into the choice of each year's winners. The awards began in Britain with the 1983 season and later reached an international audience through online voting. Their changing categories trace the growth of games: home computers and consoles, handhelds, online play, independent studios, performance and music. Alongside the public vote, special honours recognise individual contributions to the industry. Each edition preserves its own category names, so the results also show what players and the awards organisers considered worth celebrating at the time.

main.title: Resident Evil Outbreak
main.summary: Resident Evil Outbreak is a survival horror video game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation 2.

cards.text: Resident Evil Outbreak is a survival horror video game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation 2. It was released on December 11, 2003 in Japan, on March 30, 2004 in North America, and on September 17, 2004 in PAL regions. It was the first entry in the Resident Evil video game series to feature cooperative gameplay and online multiplayer support, although online support was not available for the PAL versions of the game.

Outbreak depicts a series of episodic storylines in a zombie-inhabited Raccoon City. Players control eight characters with unique abilities. It is set during the same general time period as Resident Evil 2 (1998) and Resident Evil 3: Nemesis (1999). Capcom released a standalone expansion, Resident Evil Outbreak: File #2, the following year. The game was praised for its graphics, fun factor and multiplayer, but criticized for lacking voice chat.

main.title: Donkey Konga
main.subtitle: A different kind of barrel
main.summary: Donkey Konga is a rhythm game developed by Namco for GameCube, built around the DK Bongos controller. Two small drums and a microphone turn the familiar action of following notes into tapping and clapping. Donkey Kong and Diddy provide the characters, while the music ranges across game themes and popular songs. The selection changes between regions, giving the Japanese, European and North American releases distinct musical identities. It is a party-friendly use of a dedicated accessory, with an ordinary controller also supported.

cards.heading: A different kind of barrel
cards.text: Donkey Konga is a rhythm game developed by Namco for GameCube, built around the DK Bongos controller. Two small drums and a microphone turn the familiar action of following notes into tapping and clapping. Donkey Kong and Diddy provide the characters, while the music ranges across game themes and popular songs. The selection changes between regions, giving the Japanese, European and North American releases distinct musical identities. It is a party-friendly use of a dedicated accessory, with an ordinary controller also supported.

cards.heading: Hands on the beat
cards.text: The basic pleasure comes from matching a visible instruction to a physical gesture. The two drum surfaces and clap sensor provide a compact vocabulary, leaving timing as the central challenge. A player can understand the arrangement quickly and then improve through familiarity with a song’s pattern. The controller makes those actions visible to everyone nearby, so a performance has an immediate social quality. Donkey Konga asks little in terms of buttons, but gives rhythm a more bodily presence than a conventional pad would.

cards.heading: Practice makes bananas
cards.text: The story gives the unusual instrument a suitably simple introduction. Donkey Kong and Diddy discover barrel-like objects on a beach and take them to Cranky, worried about King K. Rool. Cranky identifies the bongos, but the pair initially play them badly. His advice is to practise; the prospect of earning enough for plentiful bananas supplies their motivation. This small setup gives the music game a place in Donkey Kong’s world, turning a new controller into an object the characters themselves have to learn.

main.title: The Sims Bustin' Out
main.summary: The Sims Bustin' Out is a 2003 social simulation video game developed by Maxis and published by Electronic Arts for the Game Boy Advance, GameCube, PlayStation 2 and Xbox, with a port for the N-Gage following in 2004.

cards.text: The Sims Bustin' Out is a 2003 social simulation video game developed by Maxis and published by Electronic Arts for the Game Boy Advance, GameCube, PlayStation 2 and Xbox, with a port for the N-Gage following in 2004. It is the second title in The Sims console series, and the first title not to be concurrently released for Microsoft Windows.

The game features the same 3D environment and engine as the original Sims game, but adds several features from the expansion packs Livin' Large, House Party, Hot Date, and Superstar. As the title suggests, Sims can get out of the house to visit other locations, such as Shiny Things Lab or Casa Caliente. There are two modes: Bust Out Mode, which has mission-based gameplay, and Freeplay Mode, which is open-ended gameplay much like the original Sims game. The PlayStation 2 version once featured the option to play online; it was shut down on August 1, 2008, the same day The Sims Online shut down.
The Game Boy Advance and N-Gage version has its own storyline. The Game Boy Advance and Nintendo DS version of The Urbz: Sims in the City, released in 2004, serves as a sequel to this version.

main.title: Astro Boy: Omega Factor
main.subtitle: Tezuka’s small robot meets a much larger cast
main.summary: Astro Boy: Omega Factor is Treasure and Hitmaker's Game Boy Advance action game sending Osamu Tezuka's robot hero through a journey populated by characters from across the creator's work. Close-range fighting mixes with flight and shooting, allowing Astro's different abilities to change the pace between stages. The supporting cast gives the adventure a wider identity than a simple retelling of one television episode. Meeting people becomes part of Astro's development, connecting the action with the empathy and relationships at the centre of a hero who is powerful but still learning about the world around him.

cards.heading: Tezuka’s small robot meets a much larger cast
cards.text: Astro Boy: Omega Factor is Treasure and Hitmaker's Game Boy Advance action game sending Osamu Tezuka's robot hero through a journey populated by characters from across the creator's work. Close-range fighting mixes with flight and shooting, allowing Astro's different abilities to change the pace between stages. The supporting cast gives the adventure a wider identity than a simple retelling of one television episode. Meeting people becomes part of Astro's development, connecting the action with the empathy and relationships at the centre of a hero who is powerful but still learning about the world around him.

cards.heading: A successful attack prepares something larger
cards.text: Astro punches, kicks and uses his laser to deal with enemies, gradually filling the EX gauge through successful attacks. The stored energy powers stronger techniques, including attacks capable of affecting several opponents at once. Flight sections use his rocket abilities to change the arrangement of the action, moving from a close exchange to threats approached through the air. The abilities work as parts of one character rather than separate equipment choices. The player learns when ordinary attacks can build the resource needed and when the current group of enemies justifies spending it.

cards.heading: A meeting becomes part of the Omega Factor
cards.text: Encounters with the wider cast contribute to the Omega Factor, connecting Astro's growth with the people he meets during the journey. Character development therefore has a narrative form alongside its practical effect on the action. The game draws on Tezuka's recurring use of recognisable characters across different stories, bringing that larger creative world into one portable adventure. Its stages supply immediate threats, but the developing record of relationships gives another reason to explore what surrounds them. Astro becomes stronger through understanding and meeting others, making the collection fit the particular hero at its centre.

main.title: Front Mission 4
main.subtitle: A military crisis told through two investigations
main.summary: Front Mission 4 is Square Enix's PlayStation 2 tactical role-playing game, first released in Japan on 18 December 2003. Set in 2096, it follows two groups drawn into an international crisis involving attacks on military bases and competition between powerful states. Their battles are fought in wanzers, customisable walking machines whose parts determine their role on the field. The player alternates between the story and the work of preparing a squad. Political events become practical problems of positioning, equipment and getting several units through the same dangerous encounter.

cards.heading: A military crisis told through two investigations
cards.text: Front Mission 4 is Square Enix's PlayStation 2 tactical role-playing game, first released in Japan on 18 December 2003. Set in 2096, it follows two groups drawn into an international crisis involving attacks on military bases and competition between powerful states. Their battles are fought in wanzers, customisable walking machines whose parts determine their role on the field. The player alternates between the story and the work of preparing a squad. Political events become practical problems of positioning, equipment and getting several units through the same dangerous encounter.

cards.heading: Make the squad work as a unit
cards.text: A wanzer can be equipped for a particular task, allowing the player to think about the group as a collection of complementary machines. Movement across the battlefield determines which opponents can be reached and which allies remain close enough to help. The Link system allows units to support one another, making a coordinated formation more valuable than several isolated strong machines. Preparation therefore continues after the workshop: a useful weapon still has to be brought into the right position. The player plans a turn around what the whole squad can achieve together.

cards.heading: A familiar conflict with another musical character
cards.text: Toshiro Tsuchida directed and produced the game, continuing the series' interest in military systems and the people caught within them. Hidenori Iwasaki and Ryo Yamazaki composed its score, using instruments including the pan flute to give parts of the music a different character from earlier Front Mission releases. North America received the game in June 2004. Reviews welcomed its production and customisation while noting its complexity. Its appeal lies in the connection between those layers: a story presents the conflict, then the player has to assemble and command the machines that will confront it.

main.title: Otogi 2: Immortal Warriors
main.subtitle: Raikoh returns with companions
main.summary: Otogi 2: Immortal Warriors is FromSoftware's Xbox action game, first released in Japan on 25 December 2003. The undead warrior Raikoh returns to confront demons threatening Japan's sacred capital, this time accompanied by allies. The setting draws on Japanese legend, giving the campaign a supernatural character distinct from the machinery and military worlds common elsewhere on the console. Battles are built around movement and force, with the player cutting through demonic opponents in spaces that can be damaged by the struggle. The sequel expands the original game's cast rather than abandoning its atmosphere.

cards.text: Otogi 2: Immortal Warriors is FromSoftware's Xbox action game, first released in Japan on 25 December 2003. The undead warrior Raikoh returns to confront demons threatening Japan's sacred capital, this time accompanied by allies. The setting draws on Japanese legend, giving the campaign a supernatural character distinct from the machinery and military worlds common elsewhere on the console. Battles are built around movement and force, with the player cutting through demonic opponents in spaces that can be damaged by the struggle. The sequel expands the original game's cast rather than abandoning its atmosphere.

cards.heading: Give the next battle another fighter
cards.text: Raikoh's companions allow the campaign to be approached through more than one character. Their different capabilities change the feel of moving into an encounter and dealing with its enemies. The player must judge distance and timing while keeping the fight in motion, using attacks to break through opposition rather than waiting in one safe position. The destructible surroundings make that movement visible: a battle leaves its marks on the place where it occurred. Character choice and the physical response of the scenery help distinguish one encounter from another.

cards.heading: An unusual corner of the Xbox library
cards.text: Yuki Ichiki composed the music, supporting the game's mixture of myth, violence and otherworldly scenery. Sega published the North American edition in October 2004 and the European release in February 2005. Reviews were generally favourable, but the game reached a relatively small audience. Its later backward-compatible release on newer Xbox systems gave another route to a work that had remained closely associated with the original console. Together with Otogi: Myth of Demons, it shows an earlier side of FromSoftware's action design, before the studio's later international breakthroughs.

main.title: Sonic Heroes
main.subtitle: Three speeds in the same journey
main.summary: On December 30, 2003, SEGA released Sonic Heroes in Japan for GameCube, PlayStation 2 and Xbox.

cards.heading: Three formations in one journey
cards.text: SEGA released Sonic Heroes in Japan on December 30, 2003, for GameCube, PlayStation 2 and Xbox. Twelve characters form four teams, each controlled as a group with Speed, Fly and Power formations. Switching leader changes how the team crosses an obstacle or confronts enemies. Different campaigns vary the demands of shared environments, bringing characters such as the Chaotix and the new E-123 Omega into the adventure.

cards.heading: Switching the leader changes the action
cards.text: Speed handles fast movement and route-opening actions, Fly reaches higher places and airborne enemies, and Power tackles strong obstacles and combat. A command changes the leader immediately, letting the player alternate formations as the level demands. Running sections, suspended platforms and groups of opponents give different members reasons to take the front.

cards.heading: Four teams, different priorities
cards.text: Team Sonic, Team Dark, Team Rose and Team Chaotix share these three formations but approach their campaigns differently. Rose offers a gentler introduction, Sonic the standard route and Dark more demanding encounters. Chaotix adds specific investigative objectives. Familiar areas consequently require different priorities depending on the group being played.

cards.heading: The whole team joins the attack
cards.text: A filled gauge enables Team Blast, an attack involving all three members. Its ability to clear crowds creates a moment to spend the energy gathered during combat. Each group's animation gives the shared function its own personality, including the Chaotix's chaotic performance. The attack makes teamwork visible at the peak of a fight.

main.title: SingStar microphones
main.subtitle: Two microphones turn a room into a stage
main.summary: The red and blue SingStar microphones accompanied the PlayStation 2 singing series from 2004.

cards.heading: A voice for each player
cards.text: SingStar debuted on PlayStation 2 in 2004 with a pair of microphones, identified by red and blue. Players sang along with recorded songs, alone or together. The microphones supplied the voices to the game, while the television displayed lyrics and the notes to follow.

cards.heading: Following pitch and timing
cards.text: Scoring compared the singer's pitch and timing with the song's guide. Holding a note and placing it at the right moment set the challenge. The original wired microphones required compatible SingStar software; later wireless models extended the accessory family.
